title: The Academy of Music band and vaudeville tour
summary: He remembers a Dixieland band heard in New York, later playing trumpet in a vaudeville act, and the difficulty of returning to jazz at WSMB.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: No, no. Except, uh, I was in the Academy of Music, you know, on 14th Street one day. Yeah. And I heard a jazz band that just knocked me completely unconscious. It was a knockout. Now that could have been Red Nichols, uh, uh, I don't think Bix had come to town that early.
I doubt if it was Red Nichols. I don't know who it was.
Maybe, no. But it was a Dixieland band, a little...
Couldn't have been anything which I would consider corny, like the early Ted Lewis or... Man, no siree. The Red Loom band or anything like that?
I had a horror. You know, there were plenty of Negroes down here that played that style, Ted Lewis. Plenty, plenty of Negroes, as a matter of fact.
Yeah, not that I'm trying to insult your taste, but I mean it was really Honest to Goodness, Good Band.
It was Honest to Goodness, Good Band, yeah.
In 22 or 23 then? Along in there.

I guess it was 23, around that. Around that time. I just went in the, I think it was a vaudeville house then. Yeah, I'm sure it was a vaudeville house. And I played that Academy of Music years after that in a vaudeville troupe. I was playing trumpet for Ken Whitmer's band. Bill, somebody from the Music Box Review, a dancer on the act. Bill... Bill Seaberry. Bill Seaberry. Bill Seaberry was a famous dancer in those days in Urban Berlin's Music Box Review. Oh yeah. And then after that was over, he went on the road with this vaudeville act, you see, and I was with that. He did an act with a girl dancer, and we had a band, you know, and featured the band and various things like that. And I remember playing at the Academy of Music. But I'll never forget sitting in there that day and hearing that thing in New York. And I was studying fiddle then, too. But you know, that doggone jazz has been in the back of my mind. I was studying legitimate fiddle. And that jazz was in the back of my mind all my life. Well, you can see how quickly, as soon as I got away from teaching music, I ran right back to WSMB. Yeah. And try to get back into jazz. And it's no easy matter, after you've been away from jazz for 20 years, to get back in and try to play it. I want to tell you that. Believe you me, it's a funny thing. To go from reading everything to being entirely without music. You're playing a phrase and you wonder what in the world you're going to do next, and when you come to it, you don't do much. Mm-hmm. In jazz, you've just got to, from having played many times, you have to build up a sort of framework around which you can improvise something different all the time. But you've got to have something to fall back on in a hurry. And if you don't have that, it gives you a feeling of sureness. If you don't have that feeling of sureness from this framework that you have built up, then you're in a difficult position. That's the position I was in when I went back to WSMB. I didn't know it was going to be that way, you know, but I hadn't played, I hadn't improvised music in 20 years. And there I was exposing myself to going on the air. It's a good thing we didn't get on the air for several months and we had a chance to rehearse a little bit and I had a chance to find a little bit of my old self.
